Researchers generated and analyzed 326 high-quality whole-genome sequences from residual clinical specimens collected between August 2024 and June 2025. The investigation captured significant patterns of viral adaptation, including characteristic human enzymatic mutation signatures and structural genomic deletions. The surveillance platform was established by building upon existing SARS-CoV-2 sequencing infrastructure to monitor mpox virus transmission dynamics following the 2022 to 2023 global outbreak. Clinical samples were obtained by Labcorp across all ten United States Department of Health and Human Services regions, providing comprehensive geographic coverage of circulating viral strains. This continuous nationwide sampling framework was designed to assess shifting lineage diversity and detect emerging genetic variants in clinical populations. To process residual mpox-positive clinical specimens, the investigators deployed a Molecular Loop probe-based long-read sequencing protocol utilizing Pacific Biosciences Sequel II technology. The long-read sequencing methodology generated complete genomic profiles, allowing researchers to evaluate both conserved core genomic regions and complex variable terminal ends. The assay demonstrated high technical reproducibility across biological replicates taken from individual patients during routine testing. Genomic characterization of the dataset identified two distinct clinical specimens containing clade Ib mpox virus, detected in January 2025 and June 2025. In addition to detecting clade Ib entries into the United States, the surveillance captured evolving patterns within clade IIb, revealing twelve distinct circulating lineages. Researchers also uncovered multiple structural alterations within clade IIb genomes, specifically large deletions ranging from approximately 1.6 to 17.6 kilobases positioned proximal to the inverted terminal repeats. Mutational analysis of the recovered viral sequences demonstrated clear hallmarks of host-mediated editing driven by APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases across both clade Ib and clade IIb samples. These specific mutation patterns provide substantial molecular evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission. Furthermore, the researchers detected significantly higher rates of APOBEC3-associated single nucleotide polymorphisms per kilobase in the variable regions of clade IIb genomes compared to the central conserved core region, with a statistical significance of P less than 0.001. Analytical accuracy of the probe-based sequencing approach was verified through parallel metagenomic sequencing conducted by the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on selected clinical specimens. In addition, custom computational simulations confirmed that the long-read probe assay reliably discriminates between all known mpox virus clades and lineages, including lineages not previously documented in circulating United States samples. The authors concluded that the integrated nationwide surveillance architecture enables effective real-time tracking of pathogen outbreak evolution. Having established operational capacity for both SARS-CoV-2 and mpox virus, the genomic surveillance pipeline provides a validated technological foundation prepared for rapid deployment during potential future infectious disease emergence events. Subscribe More forecasts: Atlanta 30 day forecast Denver/ Science, Tech & Medicine Metro Denver Resident Tests Positive for Clade I Mpox, Colorado Urges Vaccination By Hailey Armstrong Published on November 19, 2026 Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment — State Mpox Case Confirmation Google Street View A metro Denver resident has tested positive for clade I mpox, Colorado state health officials confirmed, as the state joins a growing list of jurisdictions reporting the more closely watched strain of the virus. Officials are now urging people at higher risk of exposure to consider getting vaccinated, even as they stress that danger to the general public remains very low. What Colorado Officials Are Saying State epidemiologist Rachel Herlihy said the risk to the general population remains very low despite clade I mpox being detected in Colorado, and she encouraged people at increased risk for exposure to consider getting vaccinated against mpox. Herlihy also noted that the JYNNEOS vaccine protects against both mpox clades, according to 9News. Colorado state health officials have confirmed the case in a metro Denver resident and are encouraging people at higher risk to consider vaccination. Clade I is one of two main types of virus that cause mpox, distinct from clade II, which caused the global mpox outbreak that began in 2022 and continues to circulate. Public health officials are tracking clade I closely because it has only recently begun spreading within the United States, and the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment says it has historically been considered more severe than clade II. Even so, recent U.S. clade I cases have been relatively mild with no reported deaths. A National Trend of Domestic Spread The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported more than 200 clade I mpox cases across at least 31 states and Puerto Rico as of October, with the agency noting that some people in the United States have likely acquired clade I mpox domestically without a known connection to international travel. That national picture has been building for months. As of its October 5 update, the CDC put the national clade I case count at 80, according to Medscape, and by October 14 that figure had climbed past 90 cases in at least 23 states and Puerto Rico, per Medical Daily. The CDC has said cases with presumed domestic transmission had been reported in more than 10 jurisdictions nationwide, a pattern the agency says points toward a likely transition to sustained clade Ib transmission in the United States, as reported by Medical Daily. Globally, more than 300 clade Ib cases have been diagnosed in high-income countries without a single reported death, the same Medscape report notes. The CDC's own risk assessment has held steady: low for the general public, and low to moderate for men who have sex with men. Similar Cases Surfacing Elsewhere in the West Colorado is not the only state watching clade I activity turn up without obvious travel links. In California's Stanislaus County, health officials identified four recent mpox cases, and state officials confirmed two of them were clade I; three of the four patients had not traveled outside the country, the same outlet reports. That echoes a pattern seen in California roughly a year earlier, when the state confirmed three unrelated clade I cases in Long Beach and Los Angeles County among people with no international travel and no contact with one another. Who Is Considered Higher Risk, and Why Vaccination Matters Anyone can get mpox through close physical contact with someone who has it, according to CDPHE, since the virus spreads mainly through close physical contact, including sex, or indirect contact with an infected person's sores, bumps, or lesions. Brief interactions without physical contact are unlikely to spread mpox, the agency says. Men who have sex with men have been at higher risk for contracting mpox, and transgender women and gender-diverse people have also been disproportionately affected, per CDPHE. State health officials describe mpox vaccination as the best way to prevent the disease. Physicians elsewhere have echoed that message in clinical settings: infectious disease specialist Jason Zucker has advised doctors to use every office visit to offer and complete the two-dose JYNNEOS vaccine series for eligible at-risk patients, according to Medscape's report. In Stanislaus County, public health officials similarly recommended the two-dose JYNNEOS vaccine for several higher-risk groups, including gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men, Medical Daily reported. Recognizing Mpox Symptoms CDPHE lists mpox symptoms as including a new rash or bumps on the hands, feet, chest, face, mouth, near the genitals, or in the rectum, often alongside flu-like symptoms such as fever, chills, headache, fatigue, and muscle aches. The rash can resemble pimples or blisters and may be painful or itchy, and it typically goes through several stages, including scabs, before healing, the agency says. People who develop a new rash or bumps and think they may have been exposed should get tested for mpox even if they have been vaccinated or previously infected, according to CDPHE. The autopsy study was conducted on a fatal case of mpox following the global MPXV clade IIb outbreak of more than 100,000 cases. The patient had achieved viral suppression of HIV but continued to exhibit poor immune reconstitution despite more than six months of antiretroviral therapy. The clinical course was marked by progressive necrotizing mucocutaneous mpox disease that persisted despite the administration of multiple prolonged mpox-targeted therapies. To investigate the scope of the infection, the study team conducted an extensive autopsy, quantifying MPXV DNA across 76 samples collected from diverse anatomical sites throughout the body. While the highest viral burden was identified in skin and mucosal tissues, the analysis also confirmed the presence of the virus in all central nervous system tissues tested. Crucially, the researchers detected replication-competent MPXV in multiple CNS tissues, providing evidence that the virus can actively persist in these regions. Using RNA-scope in situ hybridization, the team confirmed that both neuronal and glial cells were infected by the virus. Genomic sequencing of samples obtained from body and brain tissues revealed widespread tecovirimat resistance-associated variants. By demonstrating that replication-competent MPXV and tecovirimat-resistant isolates can both infect and persist in the CNS, this case study provides essential data for future therapeutic design. In the latest survey wave, concluded in October 2026, only 8 percent of adults in the United States reported having seen, read, or heard anything about mpox during the preceding month. This figure represents a slight decline from the 11 percent observed in July 2024 and marks a dramatic reduction from the 80 percent recorded in July 2022, when the initial global outbreak drew intensive national and international media coverage. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, domestic transmission patterns have evolved since the acute surge in 2022, with nationwide case counts falling substantially while a steady baseline of infections has endured. The agency has noted that this continued low-level transmission indicates a probable transition toward endemic viral circulation within the country. Federal surveillance data cited in the report show that 1,369 cases of mpox, historically referred to as monkeypox, had been officially confirmed and reported across the United States in 2026 as of October 24. The public health agency emphasizes that the mpox virus spreads person-to-person primarily through close contact, including intimate or sexual contact, with the rash, scabs, or bodily fluids of an infected individual. Secondary transmission routes highlighted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention include physical contact with contaminated materials such as shared clothing, bedding, towels, and dishes. Furthermore, exposure can occur through direct interaction with small wild animals indigenous to West and Central Africa, where the pathogen has long been established. The survey findings stem from the Annenberg Science and Public Health survey conducted between September 22 and October 5, 2026, among a sample of 1,842 empaneled American adults. Researchers found that widespread knowledge deficits documented during their 2024 assessment remain largely entrenched, following a steep drop from the heightened public attentiveness of 2022. Overall familiarity with the viral infection is notably limited, with merely 24 percent of respondents indicating that they are somewhat or very familiar with mpox, which is statistically unchanged from the 23 percent reported in July 2024. Conversely, 76 percent of surveyed adults indicated that they are not too familiar or not at all familiar with the illness, while only 7 percent expressed worry about personally contracting mpox over the subsequent three months, compared with 5 percent in 2024 and 21 percent in August 2022. General comprehension regarding preventive medical interventions has similarly stagnated over the two-year monitoring interval. Less than half of respondents, or 44 percent, were aware that an effective vaccine against mpox is currently available, a figure virtually identical to the 45 percent measured in 2024 and substantially lower than the 61 percent recorded in August 2022. Nearly half of the public, representing 48 percent, stated that they were unsure whether any vaccine existed. Additionally, only 18 percent of participants correctly identified mpox as being less contagious than the virus causing Covid-19, essentially matching the 17 percent measured in 2024, while 62 percent admitted uncertainty, contrasting with the 41 percent who correctly understood relative contagiousness during the 2022 outbreak. Public recognition of groups facing disproportionate epidemiological risk also showed no meaningful gain. Approximately one-third of respondents, or 33 percent, correctly recognized that men who have sex with men face a higher risk of acquiring an mpox infection, mirroring the 34 percent documented in 2024 and standing at roughly half of the 63 percent who recognized this vulnerability in August 2022, with 53 percent remaining unsure. Awareness of specific transmission pathways showed comparable stagnation: 49 percent recognized that sharing bedding, towels, or clothing used by an infected patient elevates infection risks, compared with 48 percent in 2024, while 51 percent recognized the infection hazard posed by close face-to-face interaction, compared with 49 percent in the previous survey. The persistence of these public knowledge deficits presents distinct public health challenges as the viral pathogen continues to circulate. Ken Winneg, managing director of survey research at the Annenberg Public Policy Center, noted that the stability of these gaps is concerning because the pathogen itself has not stood still. Winneg underscored that as the epidemiology of mpox continues to shift over time, broader public understanding regarding vulnerable populations, viral transmission pathways, and the preventive protection offered by immunization must keep pace with ongoing disease dynamics. Despite broad stagnation across many survey metrics, the research team identified measurable gains in two specific public health domains. Knowledge that the mpox virus can be transmitted through the placenta of an infected pregnant individual rose to 29 percent among American adults, up from 21 percent in July 2024, although 63 percent of respondents still reported being unsure. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention confirms that the virus can transfer to a developing fetus during pregnancy, potentially generating significant health complications for both the pregnant parent and the infant. Concurrently, public awareness regarding recommended infection control practices improved, with 73 percent recognizing that infected individuals should isolate at home until all skin rashes have resolved, compared with 68 percent in 2024. The federal health agency specifically advises patients to remain in isolation until rashes have fully healed, scabs have completely sloughed off, and an intact layer of fresh skin has developed. Intentions to accept vaccination in the event of confirmed exposure remain robust among the American public. The survey revealed that 69 percent of adults would be somewhat or very likely to receive an mpox vaccine if exposed to the pathogen, matching the 68 percent reported in 2024, while an additional 2 percent reported having already received vaccination. Notably, the share of respondents indicating that they would be very likely to seek vaccination climbed significantly from 38 percent in 2024 to 44 percent in the current survey. Furthermore, 73 percent of respondents affirmed that the clinical benefits of mpox vaccination outweigh potential risks, compared with 70 percent in 2024, a change that did not reach statistical significance. In its clinical guidance, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends a two-dose regimen of the JYNNEOS vaccine to achieve maximum protection among recommended populations, noting that the vaccine provides substantial disease prevention and can be administered post-exposure to avert illness. The survey also assessed public susceptibility to unverified narratives and medical falsehoods surrounding mpox origin and immunization. Belief in the unsubstantiated claim that the mpox virus was bioengineered in a laboratory setting was endorsed by 16 percent of respondents as definitely or probably true, showing no meaningful change from 15 percent in 2024, with 41 percent unsure and 43 percent correctly evaluating the statement as false. FactCheck.org, an initiative of the Annenberg Public Policy Center, has extensively debunked this claim. Meanwhile, 7 percent of respondents mistakenly believed that receiving a Covid-19 vaccine increases susceptibility to mpox, statistically unchanged from 6 percent in 2024. However, 63 percent correctly rejected this false claim, improving from 58 percent in 2024, while 30 percent expressed uncertainty. Wave 31 of the Annenberg Science and Public Health survey was administered from September 22 to October 5, 2026, through SSRS, an independent research organization. The study gathered data from 1,842 adults nationwide using both web-based and telephone interviews drawn from the probability-based SSRS Opinion Panel, with post-stratification weighting applied to align results with United States adult demographic parameters. The survey carries a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points. The Annenberg Public Policy Center, established in 1993, has monitored public knowledge, beliefs, and behaviors regarding infectious diseases and health communication since April 2021, with this survey project conducted by Winneg alongside Patrick E. Jamieson, Laura A. Gibson, and Kathleen Hall Jamieson.
